newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-NEW-LOOK COMBINED HEADS OUT INTO THE NIGHT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-NEW-LOOK COMBINED HEADS OUT INTO THE NIGHT.

text.p: The men's combined event at the Alpine skiing world championships on Thursday will be the first of its kind and should see the Norwegians and the Austrians celebrating when it ends late at night.
Whatever happens there will be a new champion since the reigning gold medallist Marc Girardelli of Luxembourg is absent and expected to announce his retirement next week.

For the first time since it was created in its current form of two separate races at the behest of American television, the downhill and slalom event is all being held on one day rather than over two as at previous championships.
The combined downhill race will be first on Thursday afternoon, followed by a floodlit slalom at a time when most Italians are starting to think about sitting down to dinner.

Norway's Lasse Kjus, silver medallist in the opening super-giant slalom on Monday, must be considered the favourite as Olympic champion, 1993 gold medallist and 1996 silver medallist behind the veteran Girardelli.
Kjus also won the last World Cup combined event, in Kitzbuehel last month, ahead of compatriot and overall World Cup leader Kjetil-Andre Aamodt and Austria's Werner Franz.
The only previous combined held this season before that was at Chamonix, also in January, when Austrian veteran Guenther Mader beat Aamodt into second place.

Other Austrians in with a strong chance include Mario Reiter, slalom silver medallist in 1996, and Christian Mayer who will be using Fritz Strobl's downhill skis and is also an excellent slalomist with an Olympic bronze in giant.
The Swiss have a reasonable chance of a medal, and maybe a first world championship title since 1993, with Bruno Kernen who finished third in the Chamonix combined.
There has been at least one Austrian or Norwegian on the podium in the combined at the world championships in every year that it has been held since 1982.
The Norwegians also completed a clean sweep in the event at the 1994 Olympics on home snow in Lillehammer.
Girardelli has won three times, in 1989 becoming the first skier to retain a title at world championships.
Despite the interest in Norway and Austria, the event remains the one that the International Ski Federation (FIS) are least happy about and one which has undergone most changes.
Mader said that holding the whole event on one day was "probably the last chance to save the combined."

Created to give American television more races for their money at the 1988 Calgary Olympics, the combined has long been criticised as a paper race -- at least on the World Cup circuit where it is merely a mathematical victory.

Ironically, before the World Cup started in 1967, the combined was one of the more prestigious events. It was a British invention by Sir Arnold Lunn who created organised ski racing at St Anton in Austria in 1928.
The combined was the only gold medal event at the first Winter Olympics in Garmisch-Partenkirchen in 1936.
Many skiers now take part in it merely to get extra practice in before the blue riband downhill or the slalom.
When the combined was first held with two separate races at the 1982 championships, Americans Phil and Steve Mahre refused to take part, calling it a "Mickey Mouse" event.
Michel Vion, now the French coach in Sestriere, had no such objections and went ahead and won the gold, the last time a Frenchman has won a world Alpine title.
Since then the FIS has experimented with the format, holding the slalom first and eradicating the handicap system.
